items.title: Introducing GR00T 2: our most advanced, open System One model for robotics. It runs entirely on your...
items.content:
Introducing GR00T 2: our most advanced, open System One model for robotics. It runs entirely on your robot’s onboard compute, fully untethered, and you own every weight of it. GR00T 2 features: 

1. Long-horizon tasks: dexterous manipulation and whole-body control chained over 20+ steps and 5+ minutes, such as performing chemistry lab experiments or assembling model airplanes end to end.
2. X-Adapt: adapting from easy data sources (human wearables and simulation) and deploying zero-shot to diverse real robots.
3. Unified Cognition: native integrations with frontier agents for advanced physical reasoning, robust error recovery, and safety monitoring.

It's an open-source buffet! We are releasing not only the model weights and X-Adapt recipes (coming December), but also our agentic framework, simulation engine, annotation engine, hardware design, and even training data (100K hours, that's ~11 yrs of experience), all available today! 

Everything that moves will be autonomous. Anyone can become a roboticist. 

Lock in, build with us!

items.title: We’ve partnered with Google DeepMind to launch their Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) evaluation, a ...
items.content:
We’ve partnered with Google DeepMind to launch their Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) evaluation, a new benchmark for agentic knowledge work over complex visual files

@GoogleDeepMind’s MKA is a new benchmark requiring agents to review visually complex project files such as schematics and scans, and produce deliverables like slide decks, spreadsheets, reports, and marked-up images

Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) overview:

➤ 200 private real-world visual tasks across 10 industries: Agents work from dense visual project files including architectural drawings, engineering schematics, and clinical scans to produce deliverables including slide decks, spreadsheets, PDFs, Word documents, and marked-up images. Unlike many agentic evaluations, these inputs emphasize realistic visual complexity and domain-specificity, and are genuinely required to complete the task rather than just providing additional context

➤ Climb vs. Regression rubric scoring: Each task is graded against expert rubrics, averaging ~70 weighted criteria per task. Criteria are split into ‘Regression’ (baseline checks models should pass) and ‘Climb’ criteria (harder checks designed to separate strong models). The headline score is Climb WSR (Weighted Satisfaction Rate) - the weighted proportion Climb rubric criteria successfully completed

➤ Evaluated in Stirrup with an agentic judge: We run every task in Stirrup, our open source agent harness, with code execution, web search, web fetch, and image-viewing tools (up to 250 turns), and grade submitted deliverables using GPT-6 Luna (medium) as an agentic judge

Key MKA results:

➤ Claude Fable 5.2 leads on multimodal knowledge work: Anthropic’s recently released Claude Fable 5.2 (max) leads the MKA leaderboard with a Climb WSR of 57%, followed by Gemini 4 Carbon (high) at 54% and Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at 53%

➤ Cost per Task spans nearly 30× within 10 points of the top score: Claude Fable 5.2 averages $31.97 per task, over 5× Gemini 4 Carbon ($6.29) for ~2 extra points, and ~29× GPT-6.1 Sol ($1.11). Below Carbon, all four OpenAI models tested sit on the cost-performance Pareto frontier (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra, and GPT-6 Luna), with Claude Haiku 5.5 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro making up the rest of the frontier

➤ No single model leads across all 10 industry verticals: Claude Fable 5.2 leads five verticals (Software & Data, Engineering, Logistics & Mapping, Business, and Finance alongside Claude Sonnet 5.5), Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads Education and Construction, Gemini 4 Argon (high) leads Science, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) leads Healthcare, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) narrowly leads Law & Government

Thank you to the @GoogleDeepMind team for their work building this benchmark and collaborating with us to bring it exclusively to Artificial Analysis!

items.title: It could be vastly underestimated how much human expertise is needed to diffuse the benefits of AI t...
items.content:
It could be vastly underestimated how much human expertise is needed to diffuse the benefits of AI to the long-tail of knowledge work. I think more data companies should figure out this branding, where experts help AI companies understand how to improve the tools that make them more effective, rather than replaced.

Some jobs will be replaced for sure, but I think a lot of knowledge work is deeply interpersonal, messy, and context driven in a way where AI adoption will be a productivity boon to existing employees. We are seeing this with the demand for SWEs today.

This rebrand will serve the AI industry writ large very well, but goes against the RSI narratives of the labs as "ASI will replace all knowledge work." In some ways, the difference is more philosophical about "what is the nature of work." I believe knowledge work is much more human than the evals give credit for, and this will make diffusion take a long time. Seems like Mercor can be at the center of this diffusion puzzle.

Disclosure: Yes, I advise Mercor on trying to realize this puzzle, as I think it's super interesting.

items.title:
This is a pretty cool idea:

Let your agent simulate each potential action before picking the best o...
items.content:
This is a pretty cool idea:

Let your agent simulate each potential action before picking the best one.

The model is PAN 2, a world model from the Institute of Foundation Models (IFM). They call this "simulative reasoning".

The attached video shows an example with a surfer: same wave, three different moments to pop up. PAN 2 plays out all three, and only one of them catches the wave, so that’s the one he goes with.

The model uses Generative Latent Prediction (GLP), and here is how it works:

• In: the current scene plus an action, with how long to simulate

• Out: what happens next, as a video you can check

There are two reasoning parts:

1. Conceptual reasoning: The LLM is the backbone here. It reasons about what happens next.

2. Perceptual reasoning: A 29B LDM fills in what it looks like.

This is all open under Apache 2.0!

They provided the weights, training code, and inference code, so you can run it and build on it yourself.

items.content:
AI hacking capabilities that were restricted by frontier model guardrails just months ago are now available through open-weight models.

Factory's @varinnair warns attackers are already using custom AI agents in real-world cyberattacks:

"The open weight models have clearly caught up in terms of what they can do in terms of offensive security. Now these tools are available to anybody."

"People have started building custom harnesses like ARTEX and HexStrike, which are used in real attacks today, in the last few months."

"Mythos really scared a lot of CISOs because they realized that, okay, theoretically, models can find vulnerabilities in your system, but they hadn’t really seen a breach. That changed in October, on Black October."

"After Black October, people suddenly started realizing, 'Okay, this is actually a big deal. We need to do something with our budgets.'"
@factory

items.title: Keenable Search 1.0 takes 1st (pro, 83) and 2nd (realtime, 82) on the Artificial Analysis Search Ind...
items.content:
Keenable Search 1.0 takes 1st (pro, 83) and 2nd (realtime, 82) on the Artificial Analysis Search Index: ahead of Exa (auto, dynamic highlights) and Perplexity (medium) at 80

We benchmarked both modes of @KeenableAI's Keenable Search 1.0, pro and realtime, in our Stirrup agent harness with Keenable Search as its web_search tool to complete 1700 search-focused tasks.

At $4 per 1k searches, Keenable costs about $0.040 per task in both modes, over a third below the board median ($0.063). It is also one of the fastest products we measure: 15.0s (realtime) and 15.5s (pro) per task, 2nd and 3rd on the board.

Key benchmarking results for Keenable Search 1.0:

➤ Artificial Analysis Search Index: Keenable (pro) scores 83 and Keenable (realtime) 82, up from 67 for both modes when we first benchmarked Keenable in August, and a ~50-point lift over the same model with no search (33). Both lead Exa (auto, dynamic highlights) and Perplexity (medium) at 80

➤ DeepSearchQA is Keenable's strongest benchmark: both modes score 88 F1, 1st and 2nd of 26, ahead of Exa (auto, dynamic highlights) at 86. Pro also ranks 1st on BrowseComp (87%, level with Perplexity (medium)) and on AA-Omniscience (73%, level with Exa (auto, dynamic highlights) and Firecrawl)

➤ Fast search: realtime takes 2.3s of search time per task (2nd of 26) and pro 3.0s (3rd), against a board median of 12.5s. Each search returns in about 330ms (realtime) and 390ms (pro) on average

Key details:

➤ Setup: GPT-5.6 Luna (medium) in Stirrup, Keenable Search API with mode=realtime and mode=pro

➤ Pricing: $4 per 1k requests in both modes (public pay-as-you-go price)

➤ Cards: We disabled Keenable's search cards for testing (disable_cards=true)

items.title: AI capability progress has not clearly accelerated on public measures. That said, there is some inte...
items.content:
AI capability progress has not clearly accelerated on public measures. That said, there is some internal evidence from frontier AI companies of a potential acceleration.

In the Claude Opus 5.5 system card, a preliminary @METR_Evals assessment estimated “~1.5X overall acceleration in capabilities due to AI” inside Anthropic, with “perhaps 30% chance of 2X.”

At OpenAI, experiments per active experimenter hit an all-time high in Aug 2026, about 1.6× the 2025 level.

In a report published after our Nov 3 data cutoff, @METR_Evals now estimates that capability progress at Anthropic is about 2× its earlier rate, and that around 80% of this acceleration is due to AI.

items.reasoning: Dense with specific, hard-to-find quantitative claims from METR and frontier labs about AI-driven R&D acceleration; high informational value despite low engagement. Claude Opus 5.5 is an existing model (GA 2026-09-22), not a new release.

items.title: Factory's @varinnair warns most companies are still defending against human hackers, while AI agents...
items.content:
Factory's @varinnair warns most companies are still defending against human hackers, while AI agents can execute thousands of operations per hour across multiple systems simultaneously:

"In the last few months specifically, the tools and the techniques that attackers are using has changed quite meaningfully."

"Attackers have started using agents with custom harnesses to run large parts of an intrusion all by themselves, from finding a way in, to stealing credentials, to moving across systems."

"Agent-driven attacks today launch hundreds if not thousands of operations in a given hour, which is much more than what a human attacker can potentially do."

"These agents are also attacking multiple parts of your infrastructure in parallel, whereas if you look at how human operators behave, it's usually a lot more sequential."

"Most companies' security practices are really designed around human attackers."
@factory

items.title:
Huge AI announcements from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google in the past 48 hours.

Here's everyth...
items.content:
Huge AI announcements from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google in the past 48 hours.

Here's everything going on in AI right now:

1. The authors of AI 2027 just moved their timelines up. They now expect AI on par with the best human AI researchers to arrive in 2027, after METR estimated Anthropic is improving about 2x as fast thanks to AI. Daniel Kokotajlo gives it a 50-50 chance by May 2027 and says he's "scared, sad, and angry." 

2. Anthropic opened the investor pitch for its IPO, with shares likely trading as soon as Thursday next week. An updated filing also says it has now crossed its own safety line for AI-driven progress. 

3. OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT, a beta hub where brands can set up AI agents for shoppers, claim a verified profile, and track how often ChatGPT mentions them. Paid ads can point users to those agents too. This is like the start of SEO for chatbots.

4. Anthropic rolled out Claude Sheets and Whiteboards in beta, made Claude Data generally available, and announced Claude Meetings, an assistant that sits in on your video calls. Add those to Slides, Design, and Docs. Seems like Claude is slowly rebuilding the entire office suite.

5. Anthropic also released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 yesterday, with Fable debuting at #1 on Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, 5 points ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon. It's also 20% cheaper and up to 30% faster than 5.1. Google lost the top spot before Carbon even shipped (!)

6. Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest model, built for high-volume agent work. It ties Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Intelligence Index at roughly one-third of the cost per task ($0.14 vs. $0.41 on an average test). Meta shipped its first Muse model in April and now has an answer for every tier OpenAI and Anthropic sell.

7. Google announced 2 new AI chips coming next year: the TPU 8tx, which keeps data encrypted even while a model is working on it, and the 8i Max, which joins 2 chips into one for agents that need to hold an entire codebase in view. Google already has nearly 100 TPU customers (including Anthropic and Apple) and every available chip is spoken for. 

8. Nvidia's top lawyer reportedly emailed agents in August 2025 while they were investigating whether Singapore's Megaspeed smuggled its chips to China. The Commerce Department then halted the case and handed it to the Justice Department. Not a great week for Nvidia.

9. Adobe signed a multi-year deal with Disney to build custom AI models trained on Disney's characters and visual styles, with work already underway for theme parks, film, and ESPN. Pretty interesting to see one of the most protective IP owners in entertainment is now training its own AI models.

10. OpenAI acquired Odessia, a months-old AI trip-planning startup from Sonder founder Francis Davidson, who is joining OpenAI to work on travel. Between this and #3, ChatGPT is coming for shopping and travel.

11. France unveiled the Paris Call for AI Safety and Security, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral committing to build emergency off switches into their most advanced models. Interesting timing given #1 on this list.

Daily reminder that this is the worst AI will ever be.

items.title:
We turned these cruxes into 18 forecasting questions.

To measure acceleration, we propose a forecas...
items.content:
We turned these cruxes into 18 forecasting questions.

To measure acceleration, we propose a forecasting question on the likelihood of a “fast year”: any 12 months in which the frontier of the Epoch Capabilities Index (@EpochAIResearch) rises by 30+ points, about 2× its pace since September 2024.

An ensemble of four frontier LLMs forecasts about a 40% chance of a fast year by 2030. If a fast year happens, the ensemble gives about a 70% chance that it was caused by AI automation of AI R&D.

The four LLMs disagree substantially on the probability of a fast year. For a fast year by the end of 2030, their forecasts range from 35% (Claude Sonnet 5.5) to almost 56% (GPT-6 Astra).

The LLMs made these forecasts on Oct 29, before the new METR report was released. If Anthropic’s internal 2× pace holds and reaches public models, that would roughly match the pace of a fast year. However, the METR estimate comes with caveats. For example, part of the acceleration may reflect Anthropic catching up to the frontier, and Anthropic redacted much of the evidence that METR found most informative. See our report for more discussion.

Of course, AI companies are not necessarily neutral observers. So how close is RSI really?

In the r...
items.content:
Of course, AI companies are not necessarily neutral observers. So how close is RSI really?

In the report, we provide a comprehensive overview of AI companies’ reported data, public benchmarks, and existing forecasts. (We reviewed data up to Nov 3, 2026.)

AI acts as a highly capable research assistant, but humans still supply most of the research judgment, such as choosing which research areas to focus on.

For example, no measured part of Anthropic’s AI R&D is fully autonomous. At OpenAI, AI completed 57% of 2–4-hour tasks with no human intervention in Jul 2026 (up from 28% in Jan) and 35% of 8–16-hour tasks (up from 10%).

I think SWE jobs will be safe from AI, but not the way you think:

- AI can write code and build systems much better and faster than 99% of humans.

"Hallucinations are kind of like an iceberg."

Scaled Cognition CTO @profdanklein reveals his team r...
items.content:
"Hallucinations are kind of like an iceberg."

Scaled Cognition CTO @profdanklein reveals his team routinely finds AI hallucination rates 5x higher than enterprises believe, because most mistakes look completely legitimate:

"here's the hallucinations you see where it creates a zip code out of nowhere. But most hallucinations are very plausible. They look like they could be right."

"They're like a CX bot following a reasonable refund policy that just isn't actually the right refund policy. It looks authoritative, it looks confident, it's fluent. It's just not actually a refund policy."

"When we go into enterprises and we ask them what they think their hallucination rate is, and we check with detailed auditing, we find it's routinely five times what they think."
@ScaledCognition

items.title: Public evidence points the same way. AI agents do well on well-defined ML benchmarks such as PostTra...
items.content:
Public evidence points the same way. AI agents do well on well-defined ML benchmarks such as PostTrainBench or WeirdML.

However, they struggle with open-ended research. In the CRUX 2 open-world evaluation, AI agents got the research question of an unpublished AI paper and had to write their own paper on it. The original paper’s authors rejected all four AI-written papers. On InnovationEval, where agents try to reinvent a published ML innovation, the best agent recovered 15% of its gain.
items.author: @Research_FRI
items.summary: FRI contrasts AI agents' strong performance on well-defined ML benchmarks (PostTrainBench, WeirdML) with their weakness at open-ended research: in CRUX 2, all four AI-written papers were rejected by original authors, and on InnovationEval the best agent recovered only 15% of a published innovation's gain.
items.reasoning: Concrete benchmark evidence on the gap between structured task performance and open-ended research ability; original synthesis with specific numbers relevant to RSI feasibility debates.
items.summary_html: FRI contrasts AI agents' strong performance on well-defined ML benchmarks (PostTrainBench, WeirdML) with their weakness at open-ended research: in CRUX 2, all four AI-written papers were rejected by original authors, and on InnovationEval the best agent recovered only 15% of a published innovation's gain.

items.title: Mavria cofounder @OverReactor1776 warns America could lose its AI lead not because of weaker models,...
items.content:
Mavria cofounder @OverReactor1776 warns America could lose its AI lead not because of weaker models, but because it can't build the infrastructure fast enough:

His solution: move data center construction into factories.

"You have a K-shaped deployment model for AI."

"On one hand, you have the world's best researchers constantly releasing frontier technology out of the Valley. And then the deployment of physical infrastructure underneath it, whether that's power transmission or the data center, is significantly slower."

"If we aren't able to keep our lead, the reason isn't going to be because we’re not doing enough on the model side, it's because we’re not doing enough on the physical deployment side."

"One of the key lessons from nuclear is this. You actually can see massive improvements in construction projects by taking all of these different pieces and shrinking them down so that they're more manageable and putting as much of that into the factory as you possibly can."

"We know that by bringing data center construction into the factory, we increase reliability and speed and can also scale the amount of data center capacity that America can deliver pretty significantly."
@mavriaX

items.summary: Mavria cofounder argues America's AI lead is threatened more by slow physical deployment than by model capability, describing a K-shaped AI deployment model and proposing that data center construction move into factories, drawing a lesson from nuclear construction modularization.

 • 8.4% chance of an AI catastrophe...
items.content:
Conditional on a fast year by 2030, the LLM ensemble forecasts:

 • 8.4% chance of an AI catastrophe by 2050 (vs. 2.9% without a fast year)
 • 84.3% chance that an expert panel agrees AGI exists by 2050 (vs. 55.7% without a fast year)

If a fast year happens by 2030, the ensemble’s forecast of an AI catastrophe by 2050 is almost 3× higher.

items.content:
These guys tested an auto-tuner that optimizes the full reinforcement learning loop.

Across eight math and coding jobs:

• Training steps became faster by 1.42x to 4.93x (3.5x median).

items.title: America once added 10 GW of nuclear power every year, more than its largest proposed AI data center ...
items.content:
America once added 10 GW of nuclear power every year, more than its largest proposed AI data center would need.

Mavria cofounder @OverReactor1776 predicts the US could scale to dozens, if not hundreds, of gigawatts annually over the next decade:

"We have tremendous capability to unlock energy both terrestrially and in orbit. A lot of the things that I feel are threatening America's progress come from short-sighted decisions, some of which are well-intentioned."

"There was a time when America was adding 10 gigawatts a year of nuclear power. The largest data center in the United States that's envisioned is eight gigawatts in Ohio. And we were adding more than that just from nuclear every single year. Think about that."

"I think we are able to harness terawatts worth. Using modern technology and scaling up, I think we could be adding dozens if not hundreds of gigawatts a year over the next decade."

"But we have to want it."
@mavriaX

items.title:
TL;DR My new book is now available for purchase.

As you probably know, in February 2025, I resigned...
items.content:
TL;DR My new book is now available for purchase.

As you probably know, in February 2025, I resigned from my full-time job to become a full-time author. At the same time, I started working on a new book in The Hundred-Page Books series.

Then vibe coding happened, and I couldn't resist trying to build something this way. This resulted in ChapterPal, my AI-assisted reading and learning platform, which I've built without writing a single line of code. Today, with tools like Codex or Claude Code, it doesn't seem surprising, but when I started almost two years ago, I copied and pasted code back and forth to the chatbot window. It hallucinated solutions, rewrote what was working, refused to print the entire code, etc. It was a hell of an experience.

Last spring, ChapterPal's maintenance was automated enough to allow me to return to writing, which I gladly did.

And today, 20 months after I started, I finally finished my new book: The Hundred-Page Deep Reinforcement Learning Book.

Before sending the manuscript to print, I took a two-month break so that my brain could read it as if for the first time. For the entire last week, I was reading my book and I got chills so many times that I'm sure it's a very good book.

If you have been waiting for it, thanks for being patient. I hope you will see that the waiting was worth it.

Today, the book is available on Amazon as a paperback, hardcover, and Kindle edition, and on Leanpub as a PDF.

I'm currently preparing another hardcover edition, with different dimensions, for the rest of the online stores. For those who have my previous hundred-page books in their libraries, if you want the new hardcover book to be the same size as the previous two, you should probably wait for this non-Amazon edition to be published. I will announce this separately.

A couple of words about the book.

I liked the structure of my previous hundred-page book (the one on language models), where each chapter introduces a new algorithm that improves the previously introduced algorithms in some way. This makes the textbook read like a story rather than a collection of facts.

The Hundred-Page Deep Reinforcement Learning Book builds the subject step by step, beginning with reinforcement learning fundamentals and the Policy Gradient Theorem before developing REINFORCE, actor-critic methods, Generalized Advantage Estimation, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). It then introduces off-policy learning and derives Deep Q-learning (DQN) from first principles. The final chapter shows how reinforcement learning applies to language models, including learning from human feedback and verifiable rewards with PPO and GRPO (remember DeepSeek R1).

The book comes with complete PyTorch implementations (on GitHub), the mathematical foundations needed to understand its content (in the appendices), and pointers for further study (in the last chapter). Additional learning resources are available on the book's wiki at https://t.co/uvVdxTeoLW.

The book was read and endorsed by several people I deeply admire. The back cover contains endorsements from Long Ouyang, a co-creator of InstructGPT and ChatGPT at OpenAI and Stephen Balaban, a co-founder and CTO at Lambda.

You can find all the endorsements at the book's website: https://t.co/j901nqgVfI.

I hope you enjoy this new release in the series as much as you enjoyed the other two. I can't wait for the readers' reviews to start coming.

(The Dark Edition is coming soon!)

items.title: In our report, we cover the key points of debate, including the views of researchers who expect RSI ...
items.content:
In our report, we cover the key points of debate, including the views of researchers who expect RSI very soon and those who are more skeptical.

For example, a scenario from the AI Futures Project depicts a superhuman AI researcher in 2027. In contrast, @random_walker and @sayashk expect gradual automation of AI development instead of “a singular, discontinuous moment when recursive self-improvement is achieved.”

Why do people disagree? Broad acceleration through automated AI R&D needs three steps to happen in turn:

1. Automation: Is AI R&D automated?
2. Acceleration: Does AI capability progress accelerate sharply?
3. Breadth: Are capability gains broad?
items.author: @Research_FRI
items.summary: FRI summarizes the RSI debate: the AI Futures Project's scenario of a superhuman AI researcher by 2027 versus skeptics like random_walker and sayashk who expect gradual automation, and proposes a three-step decomposition of disagreement (automation, acceleration, breadth of gains).
items.reasoning: Useful conceptual framing that structures the RSI disagreement into testable steps; cites named researchers, adding credibility, though it is summary rather than new evidence.

items.title: Hulu used to recommend Survivor even though it didn't have the show, sending users to competitors li...
items.content:
Hulu used to recommend Survivor even though it didn't have the show, sending users to competitors like CBS.

Now Hulu's founding CTO, Yahoo SVP @efeng, is bringing that same philosophy to AI search:

"When we first launched Hulu, we didn't have any content from CBS, so, like, Survivor. But if a user was looking for Survivor, we would recommend it, we would surface that in search results, and we would link out. We wanna serve the user, even if we don't benefit."

"We've taken that exact same ethos and applied it to Scout. We don't favor Yahoo News content. We don’t favor any of our sources. If there's a great sports article on ESPN, we want the user to find that."

"What is a requirement is we do right by our user and help them find the answers and information they're looking for, no matter where in the open web it exists."
@Yahoo
items.author: @MTSlive
items.summary: Hulu founding CTO and Yahoo SVP Eric Feng describes applying Hulu's user-first search philosophy, linking out to competitors like CBS for shows it did not carry, to Yahoo's AI search product Scout, which does not favor Yahoo-owned sources and aims to surface the best answer on the open web.
items.reasoning: Insightful product philosophy from a known executive with strong engagement (~6.9K views); the user-first stance on AI search is a notable counterpoint to walled-garden trends, though it carries some self-promotional framing for Scout.

items.title: MKA tests models’ visual understanding of documents including engineering schematics, architectural ...
items.content:
MKA tests models’ visual understanding of documents including engineering schematics, architectural drawings, and clinical scans and how they leverage these to produce slide decks, spreadsheets, reports, and marked-up images.

In the below example task from the 10-task public dataset, models audit a building's plans. This includes checking sections and elevations for door and window mismatches, and reporting the findings as a slide deck.

Claude Fable 5.2 (max) takes 224 turns to complete the deliverable, including viewing images 203 times, costing a total of ~$68 for the single task.

Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 costs $6.26 per minute of 1080p video, 31% less than Gemini Omni Flash 1.1

Google prices Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 at $12.00 per million output video tokens on the Gemini API, down from $17.50 for Gemini Omni Flash 1.1.

It does not reshape the price frontier on AA-Video-T2V v2.1: MiniMax H3 (768p) scores higher at $4.80 per minute, and HeyGen Video 1 scores about the same at $2.40 per minute.

It does sit in the most attractive quadrant: higher quality and a lower price than most models on the leaderboard.

 • LLM forecasts: Several LLMs are now roughly as accu...
items.content:
We note a few key limitations of our report:

 • LLM forecasts: Several LLMs are now roughly as accurate as superforecasters on ForecastBench, our forecasting benchmark. However, we know less about their accuracy on complex questions with little base-rate information (such as questions about acceleration of AI progress). Also, we elicited the LLM forecasts before the new METR report was published.
 • Data cutoff: Our data cutoff is Nov 3. The evidence in the field is moving rapidly, and so the report doesn’t fully cover, for example, the new METR report, Epoch’s Bayesian update to the ECI, or Claude Mythos/Fable 5.2.

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: The Method's 1st EP tells the story of Zipline, the $21.5B drone company that spent a decade flying blood to hospitals in Rwanda.

• Zipline was founded in 2014, and Rwanda's president opened its first blood delivery service in October 2016
• Early on, the team recovered its drones with a bouncy castle
• A Wharton study found its blood deliveries cut deaths from severe bleeding after childbirth in Rwandan hospitals by 51%
• Zipline has made more than 3 million deliveries worldwide, and its median order in October arrived 19 minutes after checkout
• Last week, they raised $1.5B at a $21.5B valuation, nearly 3x the $7.6B it was valued at in January

@sophiadew: "I could see in a very short time from now, you just snap your fingers, you ask for a toothbrush, and a flying drone delivers it in the sky in T minus 10 minutes."

items.title: StackAI's Max Poff says dashboards have "a foot in the grave" as AI agents let users get the exact d...
items.content:
StackAI's Max Poff says dashboards have "a foot in the grave" as AI agents let users get the exact data they need without digging through static charts:

"We used to say, if you wanna work with a really convoluted Excel workbook, maybe this isn't the best fit for AI. But now, I mean, they crush it."

"One of my takes is that I think that dashboards kind of have a foot in the grave."

"Dashboards just are not that useful anymore because it captures static insights that people think will be useful to users, but then you have to slice and dice the dashboard, and even then maybe you don’t get really the insight that you want."

"With a conversational interface, you can just directly get the data you need, and then the StackAI agent maintains that data on the database layer."
@stackai

items.title: Russia and Ukraine are each expected to use 7 million drones this year, with China supplying compone...
items.content:
Russia and Ukraine are each expected to use 7 million drones this year, with China supplying components to both sides.

Neros CEO @soren_ma warns America is far behind in manufacturing drones at that scale without relying on China:

"This year Russia and Ukraine are each going to use about 7 million drones on each side."

"When you think about modern conflict or deterring modern conflict, a lot of the calculus is going to come down to a country’s ability to produce these low-cost unmanned systems."

"They are both getting a lot of those components from China, and China's benefiting from selling to both sides."

"We’re not going to be able to rely on China as a supplier of our critical defense systems, especially at volume, but we're so far behind in our ability to produce things that look like consumer electronics at scale."

"There's this huge gap that we need to get across to be able to make these things in the millions."
@neros_tech

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Amazon's Ring just launched a $250 flying security camera for your home and a $...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Amazon's Ring just launched a $250 flying security camera for your home and a $1,000 patrol robot for businesses.

• When a Ring camera, sensor or alarm goes off, the Drone Cam flies to preset spots in the house to check
• It weighs 165 grams and flies for about 8 to 10 minutes at a time
• It keeps its camera off while docked, and its propellers are loud on purpose so you know when it's flying
• Ring first showed a $249 indoor drone in 2020, but only ever sold it briefly by invitation
• The Rover Cam has a periscope camera that sees over shelves, plus a siren, light tower and 2-way audio
• The Rover grew out of Amazon's Astro robot, whose $2,350 business version was discontinued in 2024
• Scheduled patrols on both need a Ring Protect subscription

@sophiadew: " Generalizing, but a 99% efficient humanoid isn't something that's safe to have in your house around your kids and your pets."

The book is especially useful because it implements the core methods from scratch rather than treating them as black-box library calls. Readers see how self-consistency, self-refinement, Best-of-N, and training-based methods actually work, including their cost and latency trade-offs. 

The book also discusses common failure modes, including cases where refinement can make answers worse. Difficult concepts such as softmax, temperature, and top-p sampling are clarified with code-linked explanations and diagrams, while visual workflows make pipelines and scoring methods easier to follow.

items.title: Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 is stronger from a text prompt than from a start image: #6 on AA-Video-T2V v2....
items.content:
Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 is stronger from a text prompt than from a start image: #6 on AA-Video-T2V v2.1, #14 on AA-Video-I2V v2.1

From a start image, it gets better at almost everything: it improves on Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 in 19 of 20 capabilities and use cases. In most of them it is still mid-table, between #9 and #13.

Two things stand out. It is now one of the best models at keeping text readable when it animates an image (#3 in Text Rendering, from #13), and at matching sound to the picture (#5 in Audio Synchronization, from #8).

It is weakest at animating people (#12 in Human Anatomy). Camera Control is the one category where it slips, from #10 to #11.

Without native audio, it climbs from #19 to #16 on AA-Video-I2V-Silent v2.1.

➤ Text Rendering covers short and long text, 2D layout, non-lexical strings, and text on deforming surfaces.

➤ Audio Synchronization covers diegetic sound effects, background music and score, and on- and off-screen sound.

➤ Human Anatomy covers gait and locomotion, fine motor movement, facial expression, acrobatic motion, object grasping, and human interaction.

➤ Camera Control covers shot types such as close-up, aerial, POV and low angle, and moves such as tracking, dolly, orbit, crane, crash zoom, whip pan and rack focus.

items.title: On AA-Video-T2V v2.1, Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 is best at people talking and at designed content, and w...
items.content:
On AA-Video-T2V v2.1, Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 is best at people talking and at designed content, and weakest at realistic live-action footage

It is now #1 for dialogue scenes (Dialogue & Lip Sync, from #7) and #2 for stories told over several shots (Multi-Scene & Narrative, from #8). Its sound also matches the picture well: it is #2 in Audio Synchronization, where only Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 ranks higher.

It does well on designed and commercial content: #1 in UIUX & Motion Design, #3 in Retail & Ecommerce and in Animation & Gaming, and #4 in Marketing & Advertising.

It is weaker when the video must look like real footage: #8 in Live-Action Film, #9 in Consumer, and #9 in Human Anatomy, down from #8. It does better with people who talk than with people who move.

Without native audio, it climbs from #14 to #7 on AA-Video-T2V-Silent v2.1.

➤ Dialogue & Lip Sync covers single- and multi-speaker dialogue, and voiceover vs on-screen speech.

➤ Multi-Scene & Narrative covers multi-event stories, shot transitions, montage, and identity consistency across shots.

➤ UIUX & Motion Design covers kinetic typography, UI motion demos across devices, and abstract motion graphics.

➤ Live-Action Film covers cinematic shots, microdrama episodes, and previsualization.

➤ Human Anatomy covers gait and locomotion, fine motor movement, facial expression, acrobatic motion, object grasping, and human interaction.

items.content:
Another interesting area where PAN 2 really shines: multi-step plans.

Remember that when working on a multi-step plan, if you pick the wrong step, the entire plan fails.

PAN 2 got 75.1% of steps right and finished 34.0% of plans on a benchmark of 100 everyday tasks consisting of 3-6 steps.

This was the highest full-plan completion among the well-known models IFM tested, such as Cosmos 3 Super and FLUX 3.

More details: https://t.co/CGB53trcFo

items.title: Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 takes #2 on AA-Video-Editing v1.1 and improves on Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 on AA-...
items.content:
Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 takes #2 on AA-Video-Editing v1.1 and improves on Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 on AA-Video-T2V v2.1 (#12 to #6) and AA-Video-I2V v2.1 (#17 to #14)

Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 is Google's latest video model, released on November 5. It supports Text to Video, Image to Video and Video Editing, with native audio, and generates clips of up to 15 seconds. It will replace Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 on the Gemini API on December 3.

In our testing, it performs best on dialogue scenes, multi-shot stories and UI and motion design clips in Text to Video, and on complex edits and visual effects in Video Editing. It is weaker at human anatomy and at sound and speech edits.

Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 costs $6.26 per minute of 1080p video on the Gemini API, 31% less than Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 at $9.12 per minute.

It is available in the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Vertex AI, the Gemini app, Google Flow and YouTube.

Congratulations to @GoogleDeepMind on the release!

Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 is Google's latest video model, released on November 5. It supports Text to Video, Image to Video and Video Editing, with native audio, and generates clips of up to 15 seconds. It will replace Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 on the Gemini API on December 3.

In our testing, it performs best on dialogue scenes, multi-shot stories and UI and motion design clips in Text to Video, and on complex edits and visual effects in Video Editing. It is weaker at human anatomy and at sound and speech edits.

Gemini Omni Flash 1.2 costs $6.26 per minute of 1080p video on the Gemini API, 31% less than Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 at $9.12 per minute.

It is available in the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Vertex AI, the Gemini app, Google Flow and YouTube.

Congratulations to @GoogleDeepMind on the release!

It’s 2029, just before the next inauguration, Trump’s last day in office. Clinton, Trump and Biden are sitting around the Oval Office sipping beers and reminiscing.

Trump: So what’s the stupidest thing you did when you were President?

Clinton: Well I let an intern give me a blow job. In the Oval Office! People found out! I almost lost my job over it!

[laughter]

Biden: I stayed in office way too; screwed over my party, and let this guy [points to Trump] back in the White House.

[laughter]

Clinton: Ok, Don your turn:

Trump: Well I let China catch up with the US in AI, launched a stupid fucking war in Iran, and then did jack shit as AI started wrecking the planet. 

[awkward silence]

Biden: Ok, Don, you win.

items.content:
MKA deliverables include six output file types and performance varies somewhat between them, though less than across verticals.

On Climb WSR, Claude Fable 5.2 leads four file types (PDF, Word Document, narrowly Spreadsheet, and Presentation alongside Claude Opus 5.5 (max)), while Gemini 4 Argon (high) and Carbon (high) lead Image, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 leads Text Files. Word Document and Text File output tasks are the hardest outputs: no model passes 52% on either.

items.content:
We note a few key limitations of our report:

 • LLM forecasts: Several LLMs are now roughly as accurate as superforecasters on ForecastBench, our forecasting benchmark. However, we know less about their accuracy on complex questions with little base-rate information (such as questions about acceleration of AI progress). Also, we elicited the LLM forecasts before the new METR report was published.
 • Data cutoff: Our data cutoff is Nov 3. The evidence in the field is moving rapidly, and so the report doesn’t fully cover, for example, the new METR report, Epoch’s Bayesian update to the ECI, or Claude Mythos/Fable 5.2.

items.title:
We turned these cruxes into 18 forecasting questions.

To measure acceleration, we propose a forecas...
items.content:
We turned these cruxes into 18 forecasting questions.

To measure acceleration, we propose a forecasting question on the likelihood of a “fast year”: any 12 months in which the frontier of the Epoch Capabilities Index (@EpochAIResearch) rises by 30+ points, about 2× its pace since September 2024.

An ensemble of four frontier LLMs forecasts about a 40% chance of a fast year by 2030. If a fast year happens, the ensemble gives about a 70% chance that it was caused by AI automation of AI R&D.

The four LLMs disagree substantially on the probability of a fast year. For a fast year by the end of 2030, their forecasts range from 35% (Claude Sonnet 5.5) to almost 56% (GPT-6 Astra).

The LLMs made these forecasts on Oct 29, before the new METR report was released. If Anthropic’s internal 2× pace holds and reaches public models, that would roughly match the pace of a fast year. However, the METR estimate comes with caveats. For example, part of the acceleration may reflect Anthropic catching up to the frontier, and Anthropic redacted much of the evidence that METR found most informative. See our report for more discussion.

items.title: AI capability progress has not clearly accelerated on public measures. That said, there is some inte...
items.content:
AI capability progress has not clearly accelerated on public measures. That said, there is some internal evidence from frontier AI companies of a potential acceleration.

In the Claude Opus 5.5 system card, a preliminary @METR_Evals assessment estimated “~1.5X overall acceleration in capabilities due to AI” inside Anthropic, with “perhaps 30% chance of 2X.”

At OpenAI, experiments per active experimenter hit an all-time high in Aug 2026, about 1.6× the 2025 level.

In a report published after our Nov 3 data cutoff, @METR_Evals now estimates that capability progress at Anthropic is about 2× its earlier rate, and that around 80% of this acceleration is due to AI.

items.title: In our report, we cover the key points of debate, including the views of researchers who expect RSI ...
items.content:
In our report, we cover the key points of debate, including the views of researchers who expect RSI very soon and those who are more skeptical.

For example, a scenario from the AI Futures Project depicts a superhuman AI researcher in 2027. In contrast, @random_walker and @sayashk expect gradual automation of AI development instead of “a singular, discontinuous moment when recursive self-improvement is achieved.”

Why do people disagree? Broad acceleration through automated AI R&D needs three steps to happen in turn:

1. Automation: Is AI R&D automated?
2. Acceleration: Does AI capability progress accelerate sharply?
3. Breadth: Are capability gains broad?

items.title: Public evidence points the same way. AI agents do well on well-defined ML benchmarks such as PostTra...
items.content:
Public evidence points the same way. AI agents do well on well-defined ML benchmarks such as PostTrainBench or WeirdML.

However, they struggle with open-ended research. In the CRUX 2 open-world evaluation, AI agents got the research question of an unpublished AI paper and had to write their own paper on it. The original paper’s authors rejected all four AI-written papers. On InnovationEval, where agents try to reinvent a published ML innovation, the best agent recovered 15% of its gain.

items.title:
Of course, AI companies are not necessarily neutral observers. So how close is RSI really?

In the r...
items.content:
Of course, AI companies are not necessarily neutral observers. So how close is RSI really?

In the report, we provide a comprehensive overview of AI companies’ reported data, public benchmarks, and existing forecasts. (We reviewed data up to Nov 3, 2026.)

AI acts as a highly capable research assistant, but humans still supply most of the research judgment, such as choosing which research areas to focus on.

For example, no measured part of Anthropic’s AI R&D is fully autonomous. At OpenAI, AI completed 57% of 2–4-hour tasks with no human intervention in Jul 2026 (up from 28% in Jan) and 35% of 8–16-hour tasks (up from 10%).

items.content:
With RSI, current AI systems help develop future AI systems.

AI companies now say this loop has begun. In an update to its IPO filing, Anthropic claimed that, based on expected future models, it now meets its definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.”

OpenAI said it already achieved the goal of an “automated AI research intern” in Sep 2026 and targets an automated AI researcher by Mar 2028.
